newsitem.title: NORWAY: Primakov sees progress on NATO-Russia document.
newsitem.headline: Primakov sees progress on NATO-Russia document.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Monday that Moscow and NATO had made progress on a binding document guiding relations between the former Cold War foes.
At the same time, Primakov reaffirmed Moscow's opposition to the Western Alliance's planned eastward enlargement, which he said could create new dividing lines in Europe.

"I think I can say that progress is emerging regarding discussions on a number of issues pertaining to the relationship between NATO and Russia," Primakov, describing his talks on Sunday in Brussels with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, said.

In Brussels, NATO sources said the two sides had agreed on the need to set up a permanent consultative mechanism to govern future relations. Russia had expressed a preference for this to be enshrined in a document rather than a NATO-proposed charter.

"This progress has not taken any vivid shape, but we could be limited optimists. And we will continue our negotiations with Mr Solana and I expect to see him in Moscow in the first part of March," said Primakov, who was speaking at a joint news conference with Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal.
Primakov flew to Oslo for a two-day official visit to NATO's only member country to share a land frontier with Russia.

"We have had only two rounds of negotiations with NATO," he said. "There is movement as to the timing of the document. When the document is ready the signing will take place. We do not set any precise dates for when it must be prepared. If we could we would have it somewhat earlier. However we do not want to hasten its publication by worsening its quality."

NATO sources say any final NATO-Russia document could be endorsed by heads of state and government at a summit in Madrid in July at which NATO will invite some former Warsaw Pact states to join the alliance.
"Russia has taken and will continue to take a negative stance regarding the enlargement of this organisation," Primakov, speaking in Russian, said.
"We did not discuss NATO enlargement," he said of his talks with Solana. "I do not intend to provide any indulgence to the NATO enlargement during our negotiations."
President Boris Yeltsin accepted on Sunday enlargement may go ahead, but said his country's plan was to stall it as long as possible.

Primakov said an eastward expansion by NATO would mean a potential security threat to Russia, but added: "However, the gravest threat is that NATO enlargement would create new, deep dividing lines in Europe.

"Therefore, when we were offered to have consultations with NATO we agreed... not for the sake of demanding a price for changing our position regarding the enlargement. This change will not take place.

"However, we would like to minimise the depth of those dividing lines which might appear in Europe...and get guarantees which would alleviate our concerns. This in our view could be recorded in a document which must meet two requirements: it must be substantive and obligatory," Primakov said.
He will meet Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland on Tuesday before leaving Norway.
